name: Cheese pashtida with spinach + whole-spelt pasta — logged batch

source.author: Logged batch — actually cooked 2026-10-24
source.notes: A batch the user actually cooked, logged as a reference per the standing skill. Based on cheese_pashtida_spinach (the adopted spinach-optimized pashtida), with 3 handfuls of whole-spelt pasta PRE-COOKED (boiled), then folded into the batter and baked together — confirmed by the user. TOTAL batch = the full cheese_pashtida_spinach recipe (4 eggs, cottage, white cheese, whole-spelt flour, baking powder, 9% yellow cheese, 180 g feta, cream cheese, 150 g raw spinach, no added salt) PLUS 3 handfuls of whole-spelt pasta (cooked before folding in). Makes 9 slices (bulkier than the 8-slice base due to the added pasta); macros below are PER SLICE (batch ÷ 9). ASSUMPTION (not given — flag and adjust if off): '3 handfuls' taken as ~90 g DRY pasta before boiling (~30 g/handful) — the macro content (protein/carbs/fiber) is the same whether the pasta is boiled before or baked raw into the dish, since boiling only adds water weight, not nutrients; the main effect of pre-cooking is a moister, slightly heavier slice (extra water retained in the pasta) and a more reliably cooked result (no risk of underdone pasta). Estimate.

serving_desc: 1 slice (~190 g baked) — batch makes 9; pasta was boiled before folding in, which adds a little retained water vs baking it dry

ingredients.qty: 3 handfuls dry before boiling (~90 g assumed)
ingredients.note: NEW vs the base recipe — dry weight assumed; boiled and drained BEFORE folding into the batter

ingredients.qty: none — as in the base recipe

steps: Boil the 3 handfuls of whole-spelt pasta until just cooked, then drain well.
Whisk the eggs; mix in the cottage, white cheese, whole-spelt flour and baking powder.
Fold in the yellow cheese, feta, cream cheese, raw spinach, and the cooked, drained pasta.
Pour into a greased/lined baking dish and level the top.
Bake at 180 °C, top-bottom heat, same as the base recipe (~35-45 min) until the custard is set and the top is golden — no extra time needed since the pasta is already cooked.

batch_totals.note: Whole bake (9 slices), incl. ~90 g dry whole-spelt pasta (assumed amount — flag if different). Vs cheese_pashtida_spinach (per slice ~127 kcal / 12.5 g protein / 0.7 g fiber): similar protein, meaningfully more carbs and fiber from the pasta (whole-spelt pasta is a real fiber source), slightly lower calcium/sodium per slice since the batch is split 9 ways instead of 8.

him.verdict: Adding pre-boiled whole-spelt pasta turns the egg-cheese pashtida into more of a complete one-dish meal — carbs jump from ~5 g to ~11 g per slice and fiber more than doubles (~1.4 g vs ~0.7 g), while protein stays essentially the same (~12.4 g) and fat barely moves. Protein density drops a little (~8.4 g protein per 100 kcal vs ~9.9 g in the spinach-only version) simply because pasta adds calories without adding protein, but this is now a more balanced, filling dish — good as an actual meal rather than a side. Boiling the pasta first (rather than baking it in dry) is the reliable way to do this: no risk of underdone pasta, since the custard only needs to set, not cook raw starch through.
flags: ~12.4 g protein / 148 kcal slice (~8.4 g protein per 100 kcal — still strong, slightly diluted by the pasta carbs)
fiber roughly doubled vs the spinach-only version (~1.4 g vs ~0.7 g) — whole-spelt pasta is a real contributor
more balanced as a standalone meal now (protein + carb + veg in one dish)
sodium/calcium per slice ticked down slightly (same batch, split 9 ways instead of 8)
pre-boiling the pasta means a reliably cooked result — no undercooking risk like baking it in dry
suggested_mods: This is the right method — pre-boiling the pasta before folding in is more reliable than baking it dry
This works well as a full meal on its own; the spinach-only version is still the better pick when you want a leaner side
Pair with a simple salad for extra vitamin C/fiber if eating this as the main dish

her_preconception.verdict: Still a strong preconception dish — the folate from the spinach carries over almost unchanged (~44 mcg DFE/slice), and the added whole-spelt pasta brings a bit more fiber and B-vitamins on top. Protein, choline and calcium remain solid. No new safety concerns versus the base recipe (fully baked; verify the feta is pasteurized as before).
prenatal_highlights: folate from spinach carries over (~44 mcg DFE/slice)
added fiber + B-vitamins from whole-spelt pasta
protein, choline, calcium unchanged in substance

safety_advisories.note: Feta is a brined cheese — Listeria risk unless pasteurized. Baked through here (cooked = considered safe); verify pasteurized, same as the base recipe.

suggested_mods: No changes needed — this remains a good folate + protein dish for her, now also more filling as a full meal

adopted_note: Adopted 2026-10-24 as the optimized version in this family (already the furthest-optimized variant: whole-spelt flour, trimmed feta, no added salt, spinach, plus whole-spelt pasta from an actual cooked batch). Per slice (of 9, ~190 g): ~148 kcal, 12.4 g protein, 1.4 g fiber, ~44 mcg DFE folate, ~316 mg sodium. him 8 / her 8. Pasta pre-boiled and drained before folding into the batter (confirmed by user) — more reliable than baking it in dry. Supersedes both cheese_pashtida_base and cheese_pashtida_spinach for actual use.
cooking_guide: Boil the 3 handfuls of whole-spelt pasta in salted water until just cooked (whole-grain pasta can go slightly mushy if overdone — aim for al dente since it'll sit in the custard too), then drain well.
Follow the cheese_pashtida_spinach method (whisk eggs, mix in cottage/white cheese/whole-spelt flour/baking powder, fold in yellow cheese, feta, cream cheese and raw spinach).
Fold in the cooked, drained pasta last, distributing it evenly through the batter.
Pour into a greased/lined dish and level. Bake the same as the base recipe (~35-45 min) — the pasta is already cooked, so you're just waiting for the egg custard to set and the top to go golden.
Tip: drain the pasta really well before folding in — excess water from under-drained pasta can make the custard slower to set.
